voice: lowercase-plain, honest about limits; proper nouns keep their casing

questions.q: how do i ignore a device i already know about?
questions.a: open the detection and hit ignore. it goes quiet right away, no pins, no log spam, no buzzer. the list lives on the beacon itself, so it holds even when your phone isn't around. ignored devices sit under managed devices, tap to unignore. holds up to 256 devices.

questions.q: can i flag one device to keep an eye on?
questions.a: yes, hit watch (the star) on any detection. it becomes its own category and the beacon calls it out when it's near, even if it would otherwise be ignored. to star something the beacon does not already recognize, switch desert mode on so it shows up at all, star it, then switch desert mode back off: the star keeps working either way. rename it under managed devices so the log reads like your log. holds up to 256. one caveat: watching matches the exact hardware address, and phones rotate theirs every few minutes, so the app warns you when a star probably won't stick.

questions.q: can i turn individual detectors on or off?
questions.a:
yes, all of them, on the Beacon tab under detectors. flip any category and the beacon obeys straight away, no reflash: flock/ALPR, drones, body cams, glasses, trackers, network cameras. scan radios above it turns a whole radio off if you only want bluetooth or only wifi.

out of the box flock/ALPR, drones, body cams and glasses are on, and trackers and network cameras are off, because both are noisy in ordinary places and are worth switching on deliberately. the settings live on the beacon, so they survive a power cycle and keep working with your phone away.

if a category is quieter than you expect, check here first, it may simply be switched off.

questions.q: what is desert mode, and when would i use it?
questions.a: normally the beacon only calls out surveillance gear it recognizes. desert mode flips that: it reports every device broadcasting nearby, phones, watches, earbuds. it's for proof of life, sparse areas, and capturing an unknown device so a new signature can be built, or so you can star it. anything you star while it's on stays starred after you switch it off. a busy street turns it into a firehose, so switch it back off when you're done.

questions.q: does desert mode cap how much it logs?
questions.a: it keeps logging, far more than a normal session will hit. the app holds a large rolling window of recent detections, a window that moves with you, not a bucket that fills up and freezes.

questions.q: can i leave it recording without my phone?
questions.a: yes, that's the offline buffer: turn it on once and the beacon keeps logging while your phone is away, encrypted, replayed when you reconnect. one honest limit: the beacon has no GPS, so offline hits are pinned to the last position your phone shared. it's built for a stationary, deploy-and-leave spot.

questions.q: my other phone won't connect to the beacon
questions.a:
a beacon that already belongs to a phone only accepts a new phone in the first two minutes after it powers on. turn the beacon off and on, then connect within two minutes. that is the whole fix.

the phone that already paired reconnects whenever it likes, forever, and never has to do this. a brand new beacon that has never been paired is not affected at all, the first phone connects whenever you are ready.

it works this way so that someone who happens to be near your beacon cannot pair to it and read where you have been. the beacon hangs up before it can explain itself, which is why a blocked attempt just looks like a connection that will not take.

only a real power-up opens the window. a firmware update restarting the board does not, so an update cannot quietly reopen pairing to whoever is standing nearby.

questions.q: the beacon keeps restarting, or the startup sound repeats
questions.a: nine times out of ten it's the cable. the USB-C port sits recessed, so a plug can feel seated while it's a hair short of full contact. push the connector straight in until it bottoms out, firmly. swap cables before you suspect the board, and rule out a tired power bank with a wall charger. still cycling on a known-good cable? email me and i'll sort it out.

questions.q: my AirTag is right next to me, why isn't it flagged?
questions.a: on purpose, and it's the beacon working right. a tag near its owner's iPhone broadcasts a quiet 'still with my owner' signal, and the beacon holds fire on those, otherwise it would scream about your own gear all day. a tag only switches to the louder 'separated' broadcast about fifteen minutes after losing touch with its owner's devices, and that separated tag is exactly the one worth knowing about: one slipped into your bag or car.

questions.q: why did a tracker on me take a while to show up?
questions.a: a tracker you walk past isn't the thing to worry about; one that travels with you is. the beacon logs a separated tag from the first sighting and holds the buzzer for its first minute, so a tag you drift past stays quiet while the sighting still reaches the app. one limit: a separated AirTag changes its identity around 4am, so a tag riding with you overnight looks brand new in the morning.

questions.q: the map shows a camera here, but nothing is detected
questions.a: the hollow rings are the known-cameras layer, community-mapped ALPR sites. solid pins are live detections. plenty of ALPRs backhaul over their own cellular link and never announce themselves on WiFi or bluetooth, so they sit on the map but stay silent on the air. the beacon can't hear what never transmits. if something IS broadcasting and it still missed it, that's a signature gap, send the log. the map also hides mapped pins that name no manufacturer, because a good share of those turn out to be something else on the pole. map settings has a switch to show them.

questions.q: can it find a hidden camera in a hotel room?
questions.a: sometimes. switch on network cameras and it flags wifi cameras from vendors it knows, hikvision, dahua, reolink, plus ring, wyze and eufy, when they're powered on and transmitting nearby. it cannot find anything wired, on a cellular sim, powered off, or too generic to tell from a smart plug. an empty scan does not mean the room is clean, so pair it with a real physical sweep.

questions.q: how far away can it hear something?
questions.a: not far, and that's physics. very roughly tens of meters, stretching toward 100 m outdoors with clear line of sight to something pole-mounted, dropping to a few meters through walls, car bodies, or a bag. treat it as 'what is around me right now', not a neighborhood scanner.

questions.q: how long does the battery last?
questions.a: roughly 4 to 7 hours of continuous scanning, about 4 in a device-dense crowd, up to ~7 somewhere quiet. eco mode stretches it by easing off the wifi sweeps while bluetooth keeps running full-time. need all-day? the slim model runs indefinitely off any USB power bank.

questions.q: why does the battery percentage jump around?
questions.a: the battery version reads charge from voltage, not a fuel-gauge chip, so it's a close estimate. under heavy scanning the voltage sags and the percent dips a few points, then climbs back. read it as a fuel gauge, not a stopwatch: full, half, and getting low are what it's good for.

questions.q: where does my data go?
questions.a: your detections go nowhere automatically beyond your phone and your own beacon. detections are logged on the beacon and mirrored to the app over a direct connection. there is no account, analytics, or automatic detection upload. if you explicitly use improve detection or export/share a Log CSV or GPX, the selected data goes only to the email recipient, app, or destination you choose.

questions.q: why does the app want my location?
questions.a: so a hit becomes a place on a map, not just a beep. your location is used on your device to pin detections and center the map. if location is on, your phone also sends its current fix over the encrypted bluetooth link to your own board, so hits the board records while your phone is away still land on the map in the right place. that fix goes to your board, not automatically to me or anyone else. ordinary Log CSV and GPX exports can include where your phone heard a device and, for drones, the aircraft and operator positions broadcast over remote ID. those ordinary exports do not have location-removal switches, so review the file and destination before sharing. the three location switches apply only to improve detection: your observation and the operator position are off by default, while the aircraft position is on. opening the map loads tiles from a map provider (apple maps on iOS, openstreetmap on android), which sees an ordinary map request and your IP address, never your detections. say no and the app still works, you just lose the pins.

questions.q: does a pin show where the camera is, or where i was?
questions.a: for almost everything, where you were, not where the device is. signal strength tells it roughly how close you got, so the pin drops at your closest pass. the exception is drones: they broadcast their own GPS over remote ID, so a drone's pin is where the drone says it is, plus a second pin for the operator.

questions.q: do i need an account or a subscription?
questions.a: no. no account, no cloud, no fees, no telemetry. buy the beacon once, use the free app forever.

questions.q: what happens if soyboi disappears tomorrow?
questions.a: the beacon keeps working. there's no account, no cloud, and no server it depends on. the app and firmware source stay on github, forkable forever. the only thing that would stop is new signature updates.

questions.q: does it get better over time?
questions.a: yes, and for free. detection is signature based, and new surveillance hardware keeps appearing, so signatures keep coming. when new firmware lands, the app flags it and installs it over the air over bluetooth from one button, which updates both radios in the beacon in a single pass. one purchase; it keeps learning.

questions.q: is the hardware open source too?
questions.a: the app and the firmware are fully open source, and always will be. the board design itself is not published. you buy the hardware, you own every byte it produces.
